paragraphs.heading: What the term covers
paragraphs.text: Climate change today has two parts: global warming, which is the continuing rise in Earth's average temperature, and the wider effects of that rise across the climate system. Scientists keep the two words apart. Global warming means only the higher average surface temperature, while climate change also takes in its effects, such as shifts in precipitation. In a wider sense, the term also covers earlier long-term changes in Earth's climate, including those caused by natural processes over the planet's history.

paragraphs.heading: What drives it
paragraphs.text: The present rise in temperature is caused by people, above all by burning coal, oil and natural gas since the Industrial Revolution. Burning fossil fuels, cutting down forests, and some farming and industrial practices release greenhouse gases. Sunlight warms the Earth, the Earth gives off heat, and these gases absorb part of that heat, which warms the lower atmosphere. The air now holds roughly 50% more carbon dioxide, the main gas behind the warming, than at the close of the pre-industrial era, a level not reached for millions of years.

paragraphs.heading: Effects already here
paragraphs.text: The effects on the natural world keep growing. Heat waves and wildfires are becoming more frequent, and stronger warming in the Arctic has helped thaw permafrost, shrink glaciers and reduce sea ice. Higher temperatures also bring fiercer storms, droughts and other extremes. In mountains, coral reefs and the Arctic, fast change is pushing many species to move or die out. The year 2024 was the warmest on record, at +1.60 °C, in a record that began in 1850.

paragraphs.heading: Risks for people
paragraphs.text: Some changes will go on for centuries even if future warming is kept in check, including warming and acidifying oceans and rising seas. For people, the threats include more flooding, extreme heat, shortages of food and water, more disease and economic loss, and these can lead to migration and conflict. The World Health Organization counts climate change among the largest threats to global health in the 21st century. Poorer communities have caused only a small share of emissions, yet they are the least able to adapt and the most vulnerable. More warming raises these impacts and can set off tipping points, such as the melting of the whole Greenland ice sheet.

paragraphs.heading: What can be done
paragraphs.text: In the 2015 Paris Agreement, countries agreed to hold warming "well under 2 °C", but the pledges made under it would still lead to about 2.8 °C by the end of the century. Support for action is broad around the world, and most countries aim to stop emitting carbon dioxide. Fossil fuels can be phased out by cutting the subsidies they get, saving energy, and moving to sources such as wind, solar, hydro and nuclear power. Electricity made cleanly can then run transport, heat buildings and power industry. Carbon can also be drawn back out of the air, for example by growing more forest and farming in ways that store carbon in soil.

paragraphs.heading: Climates of the past
paragraphs.text: Over the last few million years, the climate has cycled in and out of ice ages. About 125,000 years ago, in one of the hotter periods, called the Last Interglacial, temperatures were 0.5 °C to 1.5 °C higher than before modern warming began, and seas stood 5 to 10 metres higher than now. At the most recent glacial maximum, 20,000 years ago, it was some 5–7 °C colder and sea level was over 125 metres lower. Temperatures settled in the current interglacial period, which began 11,700 years ago and also saw the start of farming.
